newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE--Spreads narrow after Fed rate hike.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE--Spreads narrow after Fed rate hike.

text.p: Although a rate hike by the Federal Reserve was fully priced into the market, U.S. Treasury yield spreads continued to narrow on Tuesday after the Fed raised rates by a quarter-point.

The yield curve flattened by about two basis points, with the when-issued two-year note rising to 6.33 percent after the hike from 6.29 percent late Monday. Meanwhile, the 30-year bond yield rose to 6.95 percent from 6.93 percent.
The 62-basis-point spread is the narrowest since late October, 1995.
It took some time for the market to figure out how to respond to the rate hike. At first, the market rallied, with bond prices up as much as a half-point. But it was short-lived.

The market "didn't know which way to go at first, but I think it is quite interesting that in both selloffs and rallies the curve flattened," said Nanette Abuhoff, senior fixed income strategist at J.P. Morgan & Co Inc.
Abuhoff forecasts the yield curve continuing to narrow, with the two-to-30-year spread at about 55 basis points by June.
"We look to 50 basis points as a target," she said. "Now, (the market is) playing a timing game. Does the Fed go again in May, or do they wait until July?"
If the market believes the Fed will wait until July, the market could rally somewhat until then, analysts said.
The bond is said to be well supported at around 7.0 percent, while two-year notes look to trade in the 6.30 to 6.50 percent range, players predicted.
"The front end is clear cut: you don't want to own this paper," said Patrick Dimick, U.S. Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC.

Dimick said that since the Fed indicated strong growth was a major issue, upcoming data such as March non-farm payrolls and the National Association of Purchasing Management index will be closely scrutinized.

More bond-bearish data and the Fed will raise rates again soon, he said. "The text was a strong indication that they are at the beginning of a tightening cycle and not a one-off tightening," Dimick said.
Meanwhile, the shorter end of the curve steepened true to form, with the spread between the three-month and year-bills widening to 31 basis points from 27 basis points late Monday.
The three-month bill's rate rose one basis point to 5.25 percent, while the year-bill jumped five basis points to 5.56 percent.
Players said they anticipated further gains in the year-bill rate, coinciding with an increase in yields in coupons.
